lead: A web page is not a still picture. The user clicks a button, types a letter, submits a form, or scrolls, and the browser tells the page. That signal is an event. An event handler is the JavaScript function you register to run when the signal fires. Events are how a page reacts without a reload, from a UPI 'Pay' button to a live search box. This chapter covers the terms, the three ways to attach a handler, the event object, default actions, and the capture–bubble path a single click travels.
prereq: You need: 3.1 and 3.2, because a handler is just a function you pass by name.

sections.h3: An event, a source, and a handler

blocks.text: An event is a signal from the browser that something happened: a click, a key press, a form submission, a page finishing load. The event source, also called the event target, is the object where it happened — a button, an input, the document, the window. A listener is the registration you make. A handler is the function that runs. One source can have many listeners for the same event.

items: Inline attribute: <button onclick='pay()'>Pay ₹500</button>. The browser runs the string as code when the click fires. It is quick for a demo, but it mixes markup with logic, allows only one handler, and a strict Content-Security-Policy can block it.
Element property: b.onclick = pay;. This stores one function in the property. A second assignment replaces the first.
addEventListener: b.addEventListener('click', pay);. This adds to a list, so several handlers can listen to the same event on the same element. They run in the order added.

blocks.text: Remove with b.removeEventListener('click', pay);. You must pass the same function reference and the same capture option used when adding. removeEventListener('click', () => {}) removes nothing because the arrow is a new object. Keep a named function when you plan to remove it.

sections.h3: The event object, default actions, and the three phases

blocks.text: Every handler receives an event object. event.type is the event name, such as 'click'. event.target is the element where the event started. event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running now; it can be an ancestor of the target. For a key event, event.key is 'Enter', 'a' or 'ArrowLeft'. For a mouse event, event.clientX is the horizontal distance in CSS pixels from the left edge of the viewport.

Some events have a default action: a link navigates, a form submit sends a request and reloads the page, a checkbox toggles. event.preventDefault() cancels that default. It does not stop other listeners. event.stopPropagation() stops the event from travelling to the next node on the path. It does not cancel the default action. Use it sparingly; it can break delegation and page analytics.

The browser builds a path from window down to the target. The event visits it in three phases. Capture: listeners registered with {capture:true} run from window down to the target's parent. Target: listeners on the target run. Bubble: ordinary listeners run from the target's parent back up to window. addEventListener('click', fn) without options listens in the bubble phase.

Delegation uses bubbling. Put one listener on a parent <ul> instead of one per <li>. In the handler, event.target.closest('li') finds the item that was clicked. This also works for items added after the listener was attached. The reverse direction — a child component telling its parent — is a React idea; see Unit 5.

blocks.text: Attach listeners after DOMContentLoaded, or load the script with defer. Otherwise getElementById can return null because the element does not exist yet.

figure.caption: A click travels down from window to the button in the capture phase, then back up in the bubble phase; the div's ordinary listener runs on the way back, after the button's handler.

spec.title: Capture down, bubble up
spec.aria: A click moves from window capture to div capture to the button target, then back up through the div and window in the bubble phase.

examples.question: A page contains <div id='outer'><button id='b'>Pay ₹500</button></div>. A click listener on the button logs 'button'; one on the div logs 'div'. (a) Clicking the button logs in which order? (b) What changes if the button handler calls event.stopPropagation()? (c) What if the div listener was added with {capture:true}? (d) How many lines print in each case?
steps: The event path is window → document → body → div#outer → button#b. The target is the button.
With ordinary listeners, the button's target listener runs first and logs 'button'. Then the event bubbles to the div and logs 'div'. (a) Order: button, div. Total 2 lines.
If the button handler calls stopPropagation(), the event does not leave the button for the div. Only 'button' prints. (b) Order: button. Total 1 line.
If the div listener has {capture:true}, it runs on the way down, before the target. Then the button's target listener runs. (c) Order: div, button. Total 2 lines.
examples.answer: (a) 'button' then 'div', 2 lines; (b) only 'button', 1 line; (c) 'div' then 'button', 2 lines.

traps: Forgetting event.preventDefault() in a form submit handler. The browser sends the form and reloads the page, so your JavaScript output disappears. Call it for every AJAX form.
Expecting a parent's ordinary bubble listener to run before the child's target listener. The target runs first; the parent runs on the way back up.
removeEventListener fails silently if the function reference or the capture flag differs from the one used in addEventListener.
Mixing preventDefault() and stopPropagation(). The first cancels the browser default; the second stops the event path. One does not do the other's job.

Using change for live typing. For a text input, change fires when the field loses focus or the user presses Enter; input fires on every keystroke. For a <select>, change fires as soon as the choice changes.

quiz.q: Name the three phases of an event's path.
Why can addEventListener attach two click handlers to one button where onclick cannot?
quiz.a: onclick is a single property slot, so a second assignment replaces the first. addEventListener keeps a list and runs each registered handler in order.

quiz.q: A button sits inside a div. The button has a click listener that logs 'button' and calls stopPropagation(). The div has an ordinary click listener logging 'div'. What prints when the button is clicked?
quiz.a: Only 'button'. stopPropagation stops the event before the div's bubble listener runs.

quiz.q: You render 200 table rows, each with a delete button. Compare 200 listeners with one listener on the table. Give the check inside the handler.
quiz.a: Use one listener on the table. In the handler, take const row = event.target.closest('tr'); if row is not null, delete that row. One listener uses less memory and works for rows added later.

quiz.q: A submit handler does validation but never calls preventDefault. The form has action='/pay'. What does the user see after a successful validation?
quiz.a: The browser still sends the form to /pay and reloads the page, wiping the page state.

quiz.q: A div listener handles a click that started on its child button. What are event.target and event.currentTarget?
quiz.a: target is the button, where the event started. currentTarget is the div, whose listener is running now.

quiz.q: Which event fires after the HTML is parsed but before all images finish loading?
A div is registered with {capture:true} and its child button with an ordinary listener. Give the order and the phase names.
quiz.a: The div's listener runs first, in the capture phase. The button's listener runs second, in the target phase. The div has no bubble listener.

beyond: Not for the exam. Browser events also support options such as {passive:true} for scroll and touch listeners, which promises not to call preventDefault and keeps scrolling smooth. CustomEvent lets your own code publish named events, and AbortController's signal can remove a listener automatically. Modern code often uses pointer events (pointerdown, pointermove) instead of mouse events so touch, pen and mouse share one path. Framework event systems wrap native events; React's synthetic events delegate at the root. Search for 'passive event listeners', 'CustomEvent', 'AbortSignal removeEventListener' and 'pointer events' next.
